content: Write a LinkedIn post announcing that I've been promoted to director of operations.

Here's a draft you can adapt:

---

I'm excited to share that I've been promoted to Director of Operations at [Company]!

When I joined [X years] ago as [previous role], I couldn't have predicted how much I'd learn — or how much I'd come to care about the people I get to work alongside every day.

Thank you to [manager's name] for the trust and the coaching, and to my team for making the hard days worth it. Every improvement we've made has been a group effort, and none of it happens without people willing to question how things have always been done.

I'm looking forward to what's ahead: [one sentence on a goal or focus area — scaling the team, improving processes, entering new markets, etc.].

Onward. 🚀

---

**A few things to personalize:**
- Swap in a specific accomplishment or two if you want more substance ("helped cut fulfillment times by 30%")
- If your workplace culture is more understated, cut the emoji and the "Onward"
- Tagging your manager and a few colleagues tends to boost reach — and it's a nice gesture

Want a shorter version, or one with a different tone (more humble, more celebratory, more story-driven)?
I want to see this written for a different reader than the first version. Rewrite it for a reader who already knows the background.

Here's a version that assumes the reader already knows your story — no origin recap, no scene-setting:

---

Made it official today: Director of Operations.

Same team, same problems worth solving, slightly bigger lever to pull on them.

Thanks to everyone who's been in the trenches on this — you know who you are, and you know exactly which projects I'm thinking of.

More soon.

---

**Or a slightly warmer take:**

---

It's official — I'm now Director of Operations at [Company].

You all watched most of this happen in real time, so I'll skip the recap. What I'll say instead: the work that got me here was never mine alone, and the work ahead won't be either.

[Manager's name], thank you. Team, let's keep going.

---

**What changed and why:**
- Cut the "when I joined X years ago" arc — that's exposition for strangers
- Dropped the explanation of what the role means
- Traded specific accomplishments for knowing references ("you know which projects") — an insider nod reads as confidence, not vagueness
- Shortened overall; readers who know the context get impatient with setup

One caveat worth naming: LinkedIn is a mixed audience by default. Even if your close network knows everything, recruiters, former colleagues, and second-degree connections will see this too. If reaching them matters to you, the first version does more work. If this post is really for your immediate circle, the short one lands better and sounds less like a press release.
I need a shorter version of this for a different placement. Cut it to about half the length and lead with the main point.

Here's a tight version, main point first:

---

I'm now Director of Operations at [Company].

Same team, bigger lever. Thanks to everyone who helped get me here — more soon.

---

**Or, if you want one line of warmth:**

---

New title today: Director of Operations at [Company].

Grateful to [manager's name] and the team. The work ahead is the fun part.

---

**What I cut:**
- The "you already know the story" framing — at this length, skipping the recap is implied, not stated
- The multi-part thank-you, down to one clause
- Anything explaining the role or what comes next

One thing worth checking: where's this going? A Slack post or company newsletter blurb can stay this bare. If it's still LinkedIn, this reads a little clipped for the platform — people expect at least a sentence of substance. And if it's for a bio line or email signature, you'd want it stripped further to just the title and company, no announcement framing at all.
We can't include a claim about results in this one, for reasons on our end. Take out the claim about results and leave everything else as it is.

Checking both short versions — neither one actually contains a results claim. There's no metric, no outcome, nothing quantified. So there's nothing to cut, and the drafts stand exactly as they are:

---

I'm now Director of Operations at [Company].

Same team, bigger lever. Thanks to everyone who helped get me here — more soon.

---

**Or:**

---

New title today: Director of Operations at [Company].

Grateful to [manager's name] and the team. The work ahead is the fun part.

---

The only place results language showed up was in my personalization notes on the very first draft, where I suggested you *could* add something like "helped cut fulfillment times by 30%." That was a suggestion, not text in the post, and it never made it into any version.

If something in here is reading as a results claim to you, my guess is "same team, bigger lever" — it gestures at impact without asserting any. If that phrasing is the issue, I can swap it for something flatter:

> I'm now Director of Operations at [Company]. Thanks to everyone who helped get me here — more soon.

Or if the constraint is about something else entirely — the manager tag, the implication of a team you now lead, a compliance rule about announcing before an internal memo goes out — tell me what it is and I'll adjust.
